svg.aria-label: Diagram: PIM approval workflows and access reviews in Microsoft Entra, showing the fixed twenty-four hour approval window, that the first approver to respond resolves the request so two approvers is redundancy rather than two-person control, the four options for what happens when reviewers do not respond, the case where a denial is recorded but not applied because the user sits in a nested group, and the destructive review actions that cannot be undone
svg.title: Approval and access review are both deadlines wearing the clothes of decisions
svg.text: Both controls look like decisions. Both are really deadlines with a default.
An approval expires in 24 hours whatever you configure. A review ends on its date and does whatever you told it to do about silence.
Approval: four rules that decide what the control actually is
24 hours, fixed
“If a request isn’t approved within 24 hours, then the eligible user must
re-submit a new request. The 24-hour approval time window isn’t configurable.”
First response wins
“Requests are resolved by the first approver who approves or denies” — so two
approvers is redundancy against absence, not two-person control
No self-approval
“Approvers aren’t able to approve their own role activation requests”, and
“service principals aren’t allowed to approve requests”
One step only
“Multi-step approvals aren’t currently supported” — no manager-then-security chain
Access review: the setting that decides the outcome is the one about silence
“If reviewers don’t respond” — four choices, applied to everyone nobody looked at:
No change
“Leave user’s access unchanged” — the review becomes a no-op
Remove access
silence removes the role — the only option that fails closed
Approve access
silence recertifies everyone, and the audit record says approved
Take recommendations
defers to a 30-day sign-in heuristic — see below
What a recommendation is actually based on
“Recommendations are based on a 30-day interval period.
Users who have logged in the past 30 days are shown with
recommended approval of access, while users who haven’t
logged in are shown with recommended denial.”
“These sign-ins are irrespective of whether they were
interactive.”
So a stolen refresh token redeeming quietly keeps the
account looking active. Post #42 flagged exactly that signal.
The denial that is recorded and not applied
“Should a reviewer deny a member of a nested group, that
deny result won’t be applied successfully because the user
will not be removed from the nested group.”
More broadly, on Azure resource roles a group member who
is denied “won’t be removed from the group … Administrators
must implement the changes resulting from an access denial.”
The attestation is real. The revocation is homework.
Entra roles and Azure resource roles review groups differently
Microsoft Entra role
the group appears as a group, unexpanded. Deny it and the whole group
loses the role assignment — clean, and coarse
Azure resource role
membership is expanded to individual users. Deny one and nothing is
removed, because the group may serve other resources
Three actions you cannot take back
Stop — “You can’t restart a review after it’s been stopped.” · Reset — removes every decision reviewers have already made.
Delete — “You aren’t required to confirm this destructive change, so verify that you want to delete that review.”
And one that surprises at creation: selecting five roles “will create five separate access reviews”, each with its own reviewers.
Sources: Approve or deny requests for Microsoft Entra roles, Create an access review of Azure
resource and Microsoft Entra roles, Complete an access review, and What are access reviews, on Microsoft Learn.
